Thermal barrier coatings have been employed in jet engine applications for almost 30 years.
The initial application of thermal barrier coatings was on augmenter liners to provide thermal protection during afterburner operation.
The production use of thermal barrier coatings in the turbine section has only occurred in the past 15 years.
The application of thermal barrier coatings was initially limited to stationary parts, and only recently incorporated on the rotating turbine blades.
The initial lack of endorsement of thermal barrier coatings resulted from the poor initial durability of these coatings in high heat flux environments.
Significant improvements have been made to enhance spallation resistance and erosion resistance of thermal barrier coatings.
Increased reliability of thermal barrier coatings in turbine applications has resulted from the improvements in spallation and erosion resistance.
Turbine airfoil designers are continuously challenged to increase the turbine inlet temperature capability for new products.
Maintaining cooling flow levels or even reducing them is a fundamental requirement to achieve increased engine thrust levels.
Developing advanced material systems, such as high temperature nickel based superalloys or thermal barrier coatings, is one approach to increase turbine inlet temperature capability.
Increasing the cooling performance of the turbine airfoil is the second approach to increase turbine inlet temperature capability.
Thermal barrier coatings can help insulate the metal airfoil from the hot flowpath environment, enabling increased flowpath temperatures and reduced cooling flow levels.
The perspective in this paper is from a customer's viewpoint, a turbine airfoil designer.
